newsitem.title: CHINA: Japanese banks strengthen hold on China market.
newsitem.headline: Japanese banks strengthen hold on China market.

text.p: Japanese banks are strengthening their domination of the China foreign banking sector by slashing margins to grab market share from other foreign banks, bankers said on Friday.

The Shanghai branch of China's central bank this week issued a ranking of the more than 40 foreign banks with branches in Shanghai, showing that six of the top 10 banks in terms of assets in 1996 were Japanese.
The top four banks in terms of foreign exchange loans were all Japanese, as were six of the top 10 on foreign currency deposits.
"The Japanese want to dominate the market," said a European banker based in Shanghai. "They accept very low margins because their policy is to get market share rather than make money."
The Japanese banks used to largely confine themselves to loans to Japanese-related companies in China, but have recently expanded into other areas, bankers said.
"Having polluted their own territory so that no one can make money, including themselves, they are now moving into the international market," said an American banker.
"Primarily because of the Japanese, risk in this market has now become underpriced, and that annoys everybody," he added.

The rankings issued by the central bank, the People's Bank of China (PBOC), showed the Tokyo-Mitsubishi Bank as top bank in terms of assets, profits and both foreign exchange loans and deposits amongst branches in Shanghai in 1996.
The Hongkong & Shanghai Banking Corp was number two in assets, profits and foreign currency deposits, while Japan's Sanwa Bank was number two on foreign currency loans.

A senior Japanese banker in Shanghai said the Japanese banks were acting aggressively as a result of the extremely stiff competition among themselves. There are now 11 Japanese banks with full branches in the city.
"Margins have fallen because the competition is so very strong," the banker said. "The newly-arrived banks have to give favourable conditions on loans in order to get business."

Branches of banks and other foreign financial institutions in Shanghai had a total $13.5 billion in assets at the end of 1996, a rise of 50 percent over the previous year, a PBOC report said late last month.
It said the combined profits of foreign financial institutions in Shanghai totalled $52.44 million in 1996, an increase of 42 percent against 1995.
One banker said the start of local Chinese currency business by foreign banks, expected by mid-year, would provide an opportunity for western banks to redress the balance against the Japanese banks.

"Once the renminbi (local currency) market is open, foreign banks will be able to give better services to clients," the banker said. "The Japanese specialise in medium and long-term loans, while short-term loans are currently dominated by local banks."

It is expected that foreign banks with permission to conduct local currency business will be able to borrow funds from the national interbank market for a maximum of 120 days to lend to their clients.
Eight banks have so far been approved to do restricted Chinese yuan loans and deposits and detailed regulations on the business are expected to be released soon, the bankers said.
A further seven or eight banks might gain approval for the business by year-end, they said.
